## Today's roadmap

By the end of this session you can:

1. Explain what an **agent-based model** (ABM) is, and why *location* matters in it
2. **Export** a model's world as GIS files: cells as a raster, agents as points
3. **Load, check, style and analyse** those files in QGIS

::: {.flow}
::: {.box}
**Model**
NetLogo or Mesa-Geo
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box}
**GIS file**
.asc · .tif · .geojson · .gpkg · .csv
:::

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box .fill}
**QGIS map**
style · analyse · share
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 0:30 → 2:00

- You already know QGIS. Today we add one new thing in front of it: a *model* that produces the data.
- The only new idea is the middle box: turning what happens inside a model into a normal GIS file.
- We will not write a model from scratch. We use a small, ready model and follow the data out of it.
- NetLogo and Mesa-Geo are shown side by side. Follow whichever one you use or plan to use.
:::

## What is an agent-based model?

A computer model built from many small **agents** that follow simple **rules**.

::: {.flow}
::: {.box}
**Agents**
the "actors"\
*e.g. a raindrop*
:::
::: {.box}
**Environment**
where they live\
*e.g. a landscape*
:::
::: {.box}
**Rules**
what they do\
*e.g. flow downhill*
:::
::: {.box}
**Time**
repeat, step by step\
*e.g. every tick*
:::
:::

. . .

> Nobody tells the water where the lakes are. **Lakes emerge** from thousands of drops each following one rule.

::: {.notes}
⏱ 2:00 → 3:30

- Keep it concrete: one raindrop is one agent.
- The environment is a map, the rule is "go to the lowest place nearby", and time moves in steps called *ticks* (NetLogo) or *steps* (Mesa).
- The interesting pattern (lakes) is not programmed in; it appears from many agents. That is the point of ABM.
- Other examples if students ask: people choosing where to live, farmers deciding what to plant, animals searching for food.
:::

## Why does space matter?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Abstract grid**

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 240 150" style="width:100%; max-height:34vh;">
  <g stroke="#d9e2e1" stroke-width="1" fill="#f7faf9">
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="240" height="150"/>
  </g>
  <g stroke="#d9e2e1" stroke-width="1">
    <line x1="30" y1="0" x2="30" y2="150"/><line x1="60" y1="0" x2="60" y2="150"/>
    <line x1="90" y1="0" x2="90" y2="150"/><line x1="120" y1="0" x2="120" y2="150"/>
    <line x1="150" y1="0" x2="150" y2="150"/><line x1="180" y1="0" x2="180" y2="150"/>
    <line x1="210" y1="0" x2="210" y2="150"/>
    <line x1="0" y1="30" x2="240" y2="30"/><line x1="0" y1="60" x2="240" y2="60"/>
    <line x1="0" y1="90" x2="240" y2="90"/><line x1="0" y1="120" x2="240" y2="120"/>
  </g>
  <g fill="#006c66">
    <circle cx="45" cy="45" r="7"/><circle cx="135" cy="15" r="7"/>
    <circle cx="195" cy="105" r="7"/><circle cx="75" cy="135" r="7"/>
    <circle cx="165" cy="75" r="7"/>
  </g>
</svg>
```

Every cell is the same. No real place.
:::
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Real geography**

- hills and valleys (raster)
- rivers, roads (lines)
- districts, parcels (polygons)
- a real **coordinate system**

Where an agent is decides **who its neighbours are** and **where it can go**.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 3:30 → 5:00

- Many classic ABMs run on a checkerboard. That is fine for ideas, but it has no real place.
- When the environment comes from GIS data, location changes the result: water flows differently on a real hill; people meet different neighbours in a real city.
- This is exactly where your QGIS skills become useful: the environment *is* GIS data.
:::

## The problem: outputs trapped in the model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: the NetLogo view after running Rainfall
(blue lakes on a grey landscape)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
A nice picture, but inside the model you **cannot**:

- overlay roads, rivers or population
- measure lake area or distance
- compare with real observations
- make a proper map with legend and scale bar

::: {.fragment}
**Solution:** export the model's world as **GIS files** → open them in QGIS.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 5:00 → 6:00

- Show the NetLogo view (or run it live). Ask: "Where exactly is this lake? How big is it?" Nobody can answer from the picture.
- The model *knows* the answer, but only in its own coordinates. We need to get the data out in a format GIS understands.
- This is the question for the rest of the lecture.
:::

## Vector vs raster, and what they mean in a model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
Things that **move** are usually exported as **vector points**. Things that **cover the map** are exported as a **raster**.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 6:15 → 8:15

- Vector = discrete things with a shape. Raster = a continuous surface cut into cells.
- In QGIS you see this as two different layer icons.
- In an ABM: the environment is usually a raster (NetLogo calls each cell a *patch*), and moving agents are points (NetLogo calls them *turtles*).
- Today we export both: the water raster and the raindrop points.
:::

## Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- A CRS tells GIS **where on Earth** the numbers are
- **Geographic**: longitude/latitude in degrees, e.g. **EPSG:4326** (WGS 84)
- **Projected**: x/y in metres, e.g. **UTM zone 10N (EPSG:32610)**
- Layers only line up if GIS knows each layer's CRS
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 190" style="width:100%; max-height:30vh;">
  <rect x="15" y="20" width="135" height="145" rx="10" fill="rgba(0,108,102,0.08)" stroke="#006c66" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="82.5" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#006c66" font-weight="700">Geographic</text>
  <text x="82.5" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#006c66">EPSG:4326</text>
  <circle cx="82.5" cy="108" r="40" fill="rgba(0,108,102,0.15)" stroke="#006c66" stroke-width="2"/>
  <ellipse cx="82.5" cy="108" rx="23" ry="40" fill="none" stroke="rgba(0,108,102,0.5)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <ellipse cx="82.5" cy="108" rx="40" ry="19" fill="none" stroke="rgba(0,108,102,0.5)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="82.5" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#555">degrees</text>
  <rect x="210" y="20" width="135" height="145" rx="10" fill="rgba(0,108,102,0.08)" stroke="#006c66" stroke-width="2"/>
  <text x="277.5" y="42" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#006c66" font-weight="700">Projected</text>
  <text x="277.5" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#006c66">EPSG:32610</text>
  <rect x="236" y="72" width="80" height="72" fill="#ffffff" stroke="rgba(0,108,102,0.4)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <g stroke="#e3e3e3" stroke-width="1">
    <line x1="252" y1="73" x2="252" y2="143"/><line x1="268" y1="73" x2="268" y2="143"/>
    <line x1="284" y1="73" x2="284" y2="143"/><line x1="300" y1="73" x2="300" y2="143"/>
    <line x1="237" y1="90" x2="315" y2="90"/><line x1="237" y1="108" x2="315" y2="108"/>
    <line x1="237" y1="126" x2="315" y2="126"/>
  </g>
  <text x="277.5" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#555">metres</text>
  <text x="180" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#555">project</text>
  <line x1="155" y1="110" x2="198" y2="110" stroke="#006c66" stroke-width="3"/>
  <path d="M198,104 L208,110 L198,116 Z" fill="#006c66"/>
</svg>
```
:::
::::

. . .

| You want to… | What happens to the numbers | In QGIS |
|---|---|---|
| **Set** (assign) a CRS | nothing: you only add a *label* | Layer ▸ *Set Layer CRS* |
| **Reproject** | coordinates are *recalculated* | *Export ▸ Save As…* with a new CRS, or *Warp (Reproject)* |

::: {.notes}
⏱ 8:15 → 10:30

- The most common beginner problem in this whole workflow is CRS. Spend time here.
- Setting a CRS is like writing "these numbers are degrees" on a box. It does not change what is inside. Use it only when the file is missing its label and you *know* the right one.
- Reprojecting really converts degrees to metres (or between systems). Use it when you need area/distance in metres.
- Our example data is near Crater Lake, Oregon, USA: longitude about −122°, which is in UTM zone 10N (EPSG:32610).
:::

## File formats cheat sheet

| Format | Type | NetLogo can write | Mesa-Geo / Python can write | QGIS reads |
|---|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **CSV** with x, y columns | table → points | ✅ `file-print` | ✅ `to_csv` | ✅ *Delimited Text* |
| **ESRI ASCII grid** `.asc` | raster | ✅ the only raster option | ✅ `driver="AAIGrid"` | ✅ |
| **GeoTIFF** `.tif` | raster | ❌ | ✅ `driver="GTiff"` | ✅ |
| **Shapefile** `.shp` (+ .dbf .shx .prj) | vector | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **GeoJSON** `.geojson` | vector | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **GeoPackage** `.gpkg` | vector (and raster) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ QGIS default |

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Our choice today
Raster → **GeoTIFF** (or `.asc` from NetLogo). Points → **GeoPackage** (or GeoJSON / Shapefile from NetLogo). Always keep the CRS with the file.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 10:30 → 12:00

- No need to memorise; this is a reference slide. Students can photograph it.
- Point out: NetLogo's GIS extension can only write `.asc` for rasters, and Shapefile or GeoJSON for vectors. Python can write almost anything via GDAL.
- A Shapefile is really 4+ files. If you email only the `.shp`, it will not open. A GeoPackage is one file.
- CSV is the universal fallback but has no CRS inside. We come back to that.
:::

## Meet the Rainfall model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](/assets/abm-gis/img/rainfall_elevation.png){width="100%"}

[Elevation near Crater Lake, Oregon · data: ABMGIS book (Crooks et al. 2019), CC BY-SA 4.0 · basemap © OpenStreetMap, CARTO]{.credit}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Environment:** an elevation raster, 285 × 143 cells
- **Agents:** raindrops

::: {.fragment}
- Each tick, 500 drops fall at random places
- Drops **flow downhill** and **pile up** as water
- Drops reaching the **top or left edge** leave the map
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Output we want:** *where* is the water after 12 ticks?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 12:15 → 13:45

- This is a classic teaching model from the book *Agent-Based Modelling and GIS* (Crooks, Malleson, Manley, Heppenstall 2019). A Mesa-Geo version is in the official Mesa examples and in py4abm Chapter 8.
- The map is a real area. Darker = lower.
- Ask the students to guess where lakes will form before running it.
- The edges are "outlets": water that reaches them is counted as outflow.
:::

## One simple rule

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/abm-gis/img/ch08_raster_neighborhood.svg){width="100%"}

[Figure: py4abm, Chapter 8]{.credit}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
1. Look at **my cell** and its **8 neighbours**
2. For each cell, score = **elevation + water**
3. Move to the cell with the **lowest score**
4. If that is an edge cell → **leave the map**
:::
:::
::::

. . .

Water added by earlier drops raises the score, so later drops **spread out** and lakes fill up.

::: {.notes}
⏱ 13:45 → 15:15

- Walk through the picture: the centre scores 6 + 2 = 8; the upper-right cell scores 3 + 1 = 4, the lowest, so the drop moves there.
- "8 neighbours" is called a Moore neighbourhood. NetLogo's `neighbors` gives exactly these.
- The score is not a physical water surface; it is just a simple rule. That is fine for a teaching model.
:::

**① Load**
GIS data → model world

::: {.box}

[→]{.arrow}

::: {.box}

**⑤ QGIS**

:::

- This workflow is the **same in every tool**; only the commands differ
- On the next slides: [NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo} on the left, [Mesa-Geo (Python)]{.tag .mesa} on the right
- Follow the side you use. The files that come out are the **same kind of GIS files**

::: {.notes}
⏱ 15:15 → 16:30

- This is the map of the rest of the lecture. The tracker at the top of each slide shows where we are.
- Steps ①–④ happen in the modelling tool; step ⑤ is QGIS.
- Beginners who never programmed: focus on the NetLogo side and on what goes *in* and *out*, not on the code syntax.
:::

## Same idea, two tools (and QGIS)

| Idea | NetLogo | Mesa-Geo | QGIS |
|---|---|---|---|
| one raster cell | **patch** | `Cell` in a `RasterLayer` | pixel |
| a cell value | `patches-own [ elevation ]` | `cell.elevation` | band value |
| a moving agent | **turtle** (`breed [ raindrops raindrop ]`) | `GeoAgent` with a `Point` | point feature |
| the map extent | `gis:set-world-envelope` | `RasterLayer` transform | layer extent |
| the CRS | `gis:load-coordinate-system` | `GeoSpace(crs=...)`, `layer.crs` | Layer CRS |
| one time step | `tick` | `model.step()` | (none) |

::: {.notes}
⏱ 16:30 → 18:00

- A translation table. Students who know QGIS can read the right column first.
- Key message: a patch *is* a raster pixel, a turtle *is* a point. Exporting just converts one into the other.
- NetLogo has its own coordinates (patch 0,0 at the lower left). The GIS extension keeps a link between those and real map coordinates. Mesa-Geo works in map coordinates directly.
:::

## Step ① Load GIS data into the model

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.on} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo}

```{.lisp code-line-numbers="|5|6|8|10"}
extensions [ gis ]
patches-own [ elevation water ]

to setup
  gis:load-coordinate-system "wgs84.prj"
  set elevation-data gis:load-dataset "elevation.asc"
  ; the world covers the raster's extent
  gis:set-world-envelope gis:envelope-of elevation-data
  ; raster values -> patch variable
  gis:apply-raster elevation-data elevation
end
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Mesa-Geo (Python)]{.tag .mesa}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1-4|6|7-11|12-13"}
class LakeCell(mg.Cell):        # one cell = one patch
    def __init__(self, model, pos=None, indices=None):
        super().__init__(model, pos, indices)
        self.elevation = None

self.space = mg.GeoSpace(crs="EPSG:4326")
self.layer = mg.RasterLayer.from_file(
    "elevation.asc", model=self,
    cell_cls=LakeCell,
    attr_name="elevation",
)
self.layer.crs = "EPSG:4326"
self.space.add_layer(self.layer)
```
:::
::::

Both do the same three things: **say which CRS**, **read the raster**, **copy cell values into the model**.

::: {.notes}
⏱ 18:00 → 20:00

- Click through the highlighted lines on both sides in parallel.
- NetLogo: load a CRS file, load the raster, stretch the world over its extent, copy the values into a patch variable. Our world is set to exactly 285 × 143 patches, so one patch = one raster cell.
- Mesa-Geo: `RasterLayer.from_file` creates one `LakeCell` per raster cell and fills `elevation`. Then we add the layer to the `GeoSpace`.
- Both sides set the CRS by hand. Why? Next slide.
:::

## Step ② Check before you model

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.on} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

| Check | `elevation.asc` | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 285 columns × 143 rows | NetLogo world must be 285 × 143 patches |
| Extent | lon −122.27 … −121.95, lat 42.86 … 43.01 | Is it where you expect? (Crater Lake, Oregon) |
| Cell size | 0.00111° ≈ 90 m × 123 m | Degrees are not square on the ground |
| Values | 0 – 255, NoData = −9999 | Relative height, **not metres** |
| CRS | **none** (no `.prj` file) | We **assume** EPSG:4326 and must write that down |

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
## A file without a CRS
GIS can't guess. Open the file in QGIS **before** modelling: *Layer Properties ▸ Information*. If the CRS is missing, find out from the data source, or state your assumption clearly.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 20:00 → 21:30

- This is the same check list py4abm Chapter 8 uses before building a model.
- Real data often comes with surprises. This file has no CRS and the values are scaled 0–255, not metres. The original documentation does not say more.
- Good practice: check in QGIS first, because you already know how. You can do step ② without writing any code.
:::

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.on} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo}

::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: NetLogo interface after 12 ticks
(buttons, rain-rate slider, plot of contained / outflow)

**setup** → **go** → stop at tick 12
:::

[Mesa-Geo (Python)]{.tag .mesa}

![](/assets/abm-gis/img/ch08_rainfall_run_metrics.gif){width="100%"}

`for _ in range(12): model.step()`
:::
::::

After 12 ticks: 6,000 drops fell, **≈ 5,700 stayed** on the map and **≈ 300 flowed out**. Numbers differ a little between runs and tools, because rain falls at random.

::: {.notes}
⏱ 21:30 → 23:00

- Demo live if possible: `_demo/netlogo/rainfall_gis.nlogo`. Press setup, then go, and stop around tick 12.
- The demo runs gave: NetLogo 5,699 contained / 301 outflow; Mesa-Geo 5,659 / 341 (both seed 202408, but the two tools use different random number generators). The book's GIF shows 5,706 / 294.
- Ask: where are the lakes? The picture shows it, but we still can't measure anything. So we export.
:::

## Two kinds of output

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### "How many?" (not spatial)

- one number per tick: *contained*, *outflow*
- NetLogo: **BehaviorSpace** → table `.csv`
- Mesa: **DataCollector** → DataFrame → `.csv`
- open in a spreadsheet, make a line chart

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### "Where?" (spatial)

- one value **per cell**, one location **per agent**
- patches → **raster**
- turtles / agents → **points**
- open in **QGIS**

:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Today: the "Where?" outputs
You usually want both. The "How many?" outputs are common in ABM courses; the "Where?" outputs are what connects a model to GIS.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 23:00 → 24:00

- Many beginners only save the time series and lose the map.
- Spatial output = a snapshot of the world at a chosen tick. You can export several ticks (e.g. tick 0 and tick 12) and compare them in QGIS.
:::

## Step ④a Export a raster: cells → pixels

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.on} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo}

```{.lisp code-line-numbers="|2|3"}
to export-water-raster
  gis:store-dataset (gis:patch-dataset water)
                    (word "water_tick" ticks ".asc")
end
```

→ `water_tick12.asc` + `water_tick12.prj`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Mesa-Geo (Python)]{.tag .mesa}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|2|3"}
model.layer.to_file("water_level.tif",
                    attr_name="water_level",
                    driver="GTiff")
```

→ `water_level.tif` (CRS stored inside)
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.flow}
::: {.box}
**one patch / cell** → **one pixel**
:::
::: {.box}
**the variable `water`** → **the pixel value**
:::
::: {.box .fill}
**same extent and CRS** → lines up with the input
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 24:00 → 25:30

- NetLogo: `gis:patch-dataset water` turns the patch variable into a raster. `gis:store-dataset` writes it. The tick number goes into the file name.
- Mesa-Geo: `to_file` writes one attribute of the raster layer to a GeoTIFF.
- Same size, same extent, same CRS as the input. That is why it will line up with the elevation in QGIS.
- Demo button in the NetLogo model: "4a water -> raster".
:::

## Step ④b Export agents as points

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.on} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo}

```{.lisp code-line-numbers="|1|2|3"}
let drops gis:turtle-dataset raindrops
gis:store-dataset drops "raindrops_tick12.geojson"
gis:store-dataset drops "raindrops_tick12"  ; → .shp
```

→ one point per raindrop, **all** turtle variables as fields
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Mesa-Geo (Python)]{.tag .mesa}

```{.python code-line-numbers="|1|2-3|4-5"}
drops = model.space.get_agents_as_GeoDataFrame(Raindrop)
drops = drops[["unique_id", "created_step",
               "moves", "geometry"]]
drops.to_file("raindrops.gpkg",
              layer="raindrops", driver="GPKG")
```

→ one point per raindrop, **only the fields you chose**
:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
## Clean up your fields
NetLogo also exports `COLOR`, `HEADING`, `PEN-MODE`, `LABEL`… Delete what you don't need in QGIS (*Refactor fields*), or you'll confuse your future self.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 25:30 → 27:00

- NetLogo: `gis:turtle-dataset` makes a point layer from any set of turtles, converting NetLogo coordinates to map coordinates for you.
- Mesa-Geo agents already have map coordinates, so the space can hand them over as a GeoDataFrame, and GeoPandas writes any format.
- In the demo, NetLogo's shapefile got a `.prj` that QGIS may not recognise as EPSG:4326. The GeoJSON is fine, because GeoJSON is always read as WGS 84. We fix the shapefile in step ⑤.
- Demo button: "4b raindrops -> points".
:::

## Plan B: a simple CSV with x, y

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.on} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[NetLogo]{.tag .netlogo}

```{.lisp code-line-numbers="|3|5|6-7"}
file-open "raindrops_tick12.csv"
file-print "who,moves,x,y"
ask raindrops [
  ; [x x y y] in GIS coordinates
  let box gis:envelope-of self
  file-print (word who "," moves ","
                   item 0 box "," item 2 box)
]
file-close
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Python]{.tag .mesa}

```{.python}
table = drops.assign(x=drops.geometry.x,
                     y=drops.geometry.y)
table.drop(columns="geometry").to_csv(
    "raindrops.csv", index=False)
```

Result:

```
who,moves,x,y
5450,1,-121.95139,42.87417
4282,4,-122.03472,42.90083
```
:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two traps
1. NetLogo's `xcor`, `ycor` are **patch coordinates**, not map coordinates. Convert them with the GIS extension.
2. A CSV has **no CRS**. Write it down, e.g. `raindrops_tick12_EPSG4326.csv`.
:::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 27:00 → 28:30

- Works in any tool, even without a GIS library: just write a table with x and y.
- The most common mistake: writing `xcor ycor`. Those are positions in the NetLogo world (0 to 284), so the points would land near 0°, 0° in the ocean off Africa.
- `gis:envelope-of` a single turtle returns its location in GIS coordinates.
- Demo button: "Plan B: raindrops -> CSV".
:::

## Label your outputs

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.on} [⑤ QGIS]{.s}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Keep these **with** every exported file:

- [ ] model name and **software version**
- [ ] **random seed** and **parameters**
- [ ] the **tick / step** of the snapshot
- [ ] the **CRS** (and whether it was assumed)
- [ ] what each **field** means, and its **units**
- [ ] where the **input data** came from

A good file name already helps:
`rainfall_seed202408_tick12_water.tif`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.json}
{
  "model": "Rainfall (Mesa-Geo)",
  "crs": "EPSG:4326 (assumed)",
  "seed": 202408,
  "rain_rate": 500,
  "water_height": 5,
  "steps": 12,
  "fields": {
    "water_level.tif": "retained drops x 5 (model units)"
  },
  "versions": {"mesa": "3.5.1", "mesa_geo": "0.9.3"}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 28:30 → 30:00

- Adapted from py4abm Chapter 8: record input data version, processing, package versions, seed, parameters, output CRS, field meanings and units.
- Model outputs look like "real data" once they are in QGIS. Without a label, in two months nobody knows which run, which tick, or which assumptions produced a map.
- The demo scripts write a small `*_metadata.json` next to the files. A plain README text file is just as good.
:::

## PART 3 · Into QGIS {.section-slide
   background-image="/assets/section_bg.png"
   background-size="contain"
   background-position="center"}

::: {.notes}
⏱ 30:00 → 30:15

- Now your home ground. Everything from here is normal QGIS.
:::

## QGIS ① Load your layers

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.on}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Files with geometry: drag and drop**

`.tif` · `.asc` · `.gpkg` · `.geojson` · `.shp`

::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: QGIS Browser panel with the output folder, dragging layers into the map
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**CSV: add as a delimited text layer**

*Layer ▸ Add Layer ▸ Add Delimited Text Layer…*

- Point coordinates: **X field** = `x`, **Y field** = `y`
- **Geometry CRS** = `EPSG:4326`

::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: the Delimited Text dialog with x / y fields and CRS set
:::
:::
::::

Also add the input **`elevation.asc`** as a background.

::: {.notes}
⏱ 30:15 → 32:15

- Live demo with `_demo/outputs/netlogo/` and `_demo/outputs/python/`.
- For the CSV, QGIS usually detects `x` and `y` automatically. Always check the CRS box: QGIS cannot know it from the CSV.
- Load the elevation raster too, so we can see water on top of terrain.
- Menu names here are from QGIS 3.x/4.x; check them against your installed version when taking screenshots.
:::

## QGIS ② Check CRS and alignment

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.on}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
1. *Layer Properties ▸ Information*: what CRS does each layer have?
2. Unknown or odd CRS, but you **know** it is WGS 84?
   Right-click ▸ *Layer CRS ▸ Set Layer CRS* → `EPSG:4326`
3. Add a basemap: *Browser ▸ XYZ Tiles ▸ OpenStreetMap*
4. Do the water pixels and raindrop points sit **on top of each other**?

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Layers don't line up?
It is almost always the CRS. Check every layer, one by one. NetLogo's Shapefile `.prj` may show up as a *custom* CRS: set it to EPSG:4326.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: water raster + raindrop points + elevation over the OSM basemap, zoomed in so points sit on blue pixels
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 32:15 → 34:15

- Reconnect to the CRS slide: here we *set* the CRS (label), we do not reproject, because the numbers are already degrees.
- The status bar at the bottom right shows the project CRS. QGIS reprojects layers on the fly for display, but only if each layer's own CRS is correct.
- Zoom in on a lake: every raindrop point should sit on a blue water pixel. If they are shifted or far away, it is a CRS or coordinate problem (see the `xcor`/`ycor` trap).
:::

## QGIS ③ Style it

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.on}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| Layer | Symbology |
|---|---|
| `elevation.asc` | **Hillshade**, with a **Singleband pseudocolor** copy on top at 50 % opacity |
| `water_level.tif` | **Singleband pseudocolor**, *Blues*; *Transparency*: add `0` as no data |
| `raindrops` | small **simple markers**, or the **Heatmap** renderer |
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: before (grey default rasters) → after (hillshade + blue lakes + raindrops)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 34:15 → 36:30

- Default raster styling is grey and hard to read. Two changes make a big difference.
- Making 0 transparent means dry cells disappear and only lakes show, so the terrain stays visible underneath.
- Heatmap renderer on 5,700 points gives a quick "where do drops gather" picture.
- Save the style (*Style ▸ Save Default*) so the next export of the same model looks the same.
:::

## QGIS ④ Simple spatial analysis

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.on}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**How much of the area is under water?**

1. *Raster ▸ Raster Calculator*: `"water_level@1" > 0` → a 0/1 wet mask
2. For m²: *Warp (Reproject)* the mask to **EPSG:32610**
3. *Processing ▸ Raster layer unique values report*: count and area of wet cells

**Where do raindrops gather?**

4. *Processing ▸ Heatmap (Kernel Density Estimation)* on the raindrop points
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: wet-cell mask and the unique-values report with area
:::

**Do the two tools agree?** Put the NetLogo and Mesa-Geo water layers side by side: same lakes, slightly different drops.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 36:30 → 39:00

- The demo run has about 5,400–5,500 wet cells out of 40,755 (≈ 13 %).
- Why reproject: cell sizes in degrees are not metres. Area in degrees² is meaningless. This is the "reproject" operation from the CRS slide.
- Comparing tools: patterns should match (same rule, same terrain), individual drops won't (random rain). This is a nice way to show that model outputs are *one possible run*.
- Optional extension: run the model with different `rain-rate` values and compare wet area.
:::

## A vector example: GeoSchelling in Washington, DC

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](/assets/abm-gis/img/ch08_geoschelling_run_metrics.gif){width="100%"}

[Model and figure: py4abm Chapter 8 · tracts: U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line 2025 · basemap © OpenStreetMap, CARTO]{.credit}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Agents:** people (points) of group A or B, living in census tracts (polygons)
- **Rule:** unhappy if fewer than 50 % of my tract is my group → move

::: {.fragment}
Exported: `geoschelling.gpkg` with `regions_step00`, `regions_final`

1. *Symbology ▸ Graduated* on **`a_share`**, a diverging colour ramp
2. Copy the style to the other layer, then compare the two maps
3. *Basic statistics for fields*: spread of `a_share` grows from **0.31 → 0.49**
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 39:00 → 41:00

- Same workflow, but now the model world is polygons, not a raster. Export was done with GeoPandas (`to_file(..., driver="GPKG")`), see `_demo/python/export_geoschelling.py`.
- `a_share` = share of group A in each tract. At step 0 it is mixed; at the end (step 10) most tracts are almost all A or all B. The standard deviation shows it as one number: 0.31 → 0.49.
- Exporting two snapshots (start and end) and comparing them is a very common and very useful pattern.
- In QGIS, right-click a layer ▸ *Styles ▸ Copy Style*, then *Paste Style* on the other.
:::

::: {.steps}
[① Load]{.s} [② Check]{.s} [③ Run]{.s} [④ Export]{.s} [⑤ QGIS]{.on}
:::

:::: {.columns}

*Project ▸ New Print Layout…*

- [ ] map
- [ ] title: *what, where, which tick*
- [ ] legend
- [ ] scale bar and north arrow
- [ ] credits: data sources, model, seed, software

*Layout ▸ Export as Image / PDF*
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.placeholder}
Screenshot: finished print layout, "Simulated lakes after 12 ticks of rain, Crater Lake area", with legend, scale bar, north arrow and credits
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
⏱ 41:00 → 43:00

- A map made from model output must say it is *simulated*. Put "model output" in the title or subtitle.
- Credits line example: "Elevation: ABMGIS (Crooks et al. 2019), CC BY-SA 4.0 · Basemap © OpenStreetMap contributors · Rainfall model, NetLogo 6.4 / Mesa-Geo 0.9.3, seed 202408, tick 12".
- This connects back to "Label your outputs": the metadata ends up on the map.
:::
